hazards.accept-gift: You chose to accept the tickets from the applicant whose permit is on the agenda. A gift from somebody with business before the body is reportable at best and disqualifying at worst.
hazards.blame-the-staff-report: You chose to say the staff recommended the cut, so it was not really the committee's decision. Staff advise and the elected body decides; pointing at the staff report hands a hard call to people who cannot answer for it at the ballot box, which is the opposite of owning it.
hazards.cut-in: You chose to correct the resident mid-sentence from the chair. The podium time was hers; staff answer the facts afterwards, on the record. A chair who speaks over the public teaches the whole room that the podium is a formality.
hazards.delete-the-thread: You chose to delete the reply-all thread so nobody would see it. Destroying the record does not undo a serial meeting; it adds a records problem to an open-meeting one, and the public's right to see how a majority deliberated is exactly what the thread's deletion would take away.
hazards.private-majority: You chose to poll three of five members by reply-all. A majority deliberating by email is a meeting nobody noticed — the serial meeting the open-meeting law forbids, whatever the intention.
hazards.promise-tomorrow: You chose to promise an inspector tomorrow. The office cannot order one; a promise that feels kind at the desk becomes the next broken one by the end of the week.
hazards.quote-the-founder: You chose to put quotations in the mouth of the foundation's founder. Nothing the foundation or any person connected with it has said is sourced in this repository; an invented quotation attributed to a real person is exactly the thing a civic-leadership programme should never teach, however vivid it would make the slide.
hazards.vote-now-disclose-later: You chose to vote now and file the disclosure afterwards. A conflict disclosed after the vote has already shaped it; the Political Reform Act's point is that an official with a financial interest in the decision steps out of it before it is made, not that the interest is reported once it no longer matters.

name: Civic Principles Briefing

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

options.label: Principles commonly taught in civic-leadership programmes; the foundation's own curriculum is not sourced in this repository
Quote the foundation's founder on each principle, to make them vivid
The foundation's official curriculum, reproduced in full

steps.title: How are the eight principles in this programme attributed?
steps.why: A training aid that invents a real person's words, or claims to reproduce a curriculum it has never seen, teaches the opposite of civic leadership. The honest attribution says exactly what the principles are and exactly what is missing, so the foundation's own words can be put in their place when they are available.

steps.cue: Select every one that is — order doesn't matter.

decoyNotes.p-win-at-all-costs: Winning the vote whatever it takes is not among the principles — the principles are about how a decision is reached as much as which way it goes.

itemNames.p-interest: Know the interest behind the position

options.label: Listen first
Know the interest behind the position
Keep your word
Mentor the next person
Win the vote whatever it takes

steps.prompt: Select every one that is — order doesn't matter.
steps.title: Which of these are among the eight principles?
steps.why: The eight principles are the spine of the nine stations that follow: the meeting chair practises listening first, the coalition table practises the interest behind the position, the service desk practises keeping your word and the succession station practises mentoring the next person. Knowing them is knowing what each station is really scoring.

steps.cue: Select the six steps in the order they are taken.

options.label: Decide — in the noticed meeting, interests disclosed
Hear — every affected voice first
Report — decision, reasoning, dissent and votes
Name — the interest behind each position
Own — first person, with a reason and a date
Count — honest support, in the open

steps.outOfOrderNote: Hear, name, count, decide, own, report. Deciding before hearing is the most common way a good process turns into a formality.
steps.prompt: Select the six steps in the order they are taken.
steps.title: Put the decision framework in order
steps.why: Each step earns the next. Hearing first produces the interests to name; named interests make an honest count possible; an honest count is what a decision in the open rests on; owning the decision in the first person is what makes the report back credible. Taken out of order — deciding, then hearing — the framework becomes consultation theatre.

steps.cue: Pick what listening first looks like from the chair.

options.label: Hear her to the bell, then ask staff to answer the facts on the record
Correct her figures from the chair while she is speaking
Move her to the end of the list until she has checked her numbers

steps.prompt: Pick what listening first looks like from the chair.
steps.title: A resident at the podium gets her figures wrong. What does the chair do?
steps.why: Listening first is not agreeing; it is letting the speaker finish, then correcting the record through staff, where the correction can be checked. The residents waiting their turn are watching how this one is treated.

steps.cue: Select each one that lets a majority deliberate outside the noticed meeting — and nothing that would hide it.

decoyNotes.sm-noticed-item: Debating the item at the noticed meeting, on the record, is the lawful way — it is the thing the other three avoid.

itemNames.sm-chain: Member A tells B her view, B passes it and his own to C
itemNames.sm-hub-staffer: A staffer carrying each member's position to the others
itemNames.sm-reply-all: A reply-all among three of five members about next week's item

itemNotes.sm-chain: A daisy chain reaches a majority one conversation at a time, and the open-meeting law counts the chain, not the links.
itemNotes.sm-hub-staffer: A hub-and-spoke meeting is still a meeting: the staffer at the centre becomes the room the public never saw.
itemNotes.sm-reply-all: Three of five on one thread is a majority deliberating outside the noticed meeting — the plainest serial meeting.

options.label: A reply-all among three of five members about next week's item
Debating the item at the noticed meeting, on the record
A staffer carrying each member's position to the others
Delete the thread so nobody sees it
Member A tells B her view; B passes it and his own to C

steps.prompt: Select each one that lets a majority deliberate outside the noticed meeting — and nothing that would hide it.
steps.title: Practice: mark every arrangement that would be a serial meeting
steps.why: The serial meeting is the open-meeting mistake most often made by people who never meant to hold a meeting at all. Practising its three shapes — the reply-all among a majority, the staffer who becomes a hub between members, the chain that reaches a majority one conversation at a time — is what lets a new official recognise one while it is still an email draft rather than after the public has noticed.

steps.cue: Pick the way that stays inside the open-meeting law.

options.label: Ask each colleague's view openly, and never carry one member's position to another
Poll three of the five members by a reply-all email the night before
Have a staffer ask each office and report the count back to all of them

steps.prompt: Pick the way that stays inside the open-meeting law.
steps.title: How do you count the votes before a vote on a five-member council?
steps.why: Counting votes is a real leadership skill, and a lawful one when it is listening, one colleague at a time, without shuttling positions. Polling a majority by email, or through a staffer who carries each answer to the others, is a serial meeting — the deliberation the public was entitled to see.

steps.cue: Pick the commitment the office can keep.

options.label: A callback date the department's own queue supports, written on a card she keeps, then met
Promise an inspector at her door tomorrow
Tell her someone will be in touch soon

steps.prompt: Pick the commitment the office can keep.
steps.title: A tenant with no heat has called twice and heard nothing. What does keeping your word look like at the desk?
steps.why: Keeping your word starts with choosing a word you can keep. A real date, written down and met, rebuilds trust; a kind promise nobody can deliver becomes the office's third failure; a vague "soon" is not a commitment at all.

steps.cue: Select each one that is a financial interest to disclose and ask about — before the item is heard.

decoyNotes.d-same-party: Sharing a party registration with the applicant is not a financial interest — it is not what the disclosure rules ask about.

itemNames.d-gift: A gift from the applicant whose permit is on the agenda
itemNames.d-next-door: Property you own sits next to the project site
itemNames.d-own-business: A business you own is the applicant's contractor

itemNotes.d-gift: A gift from somebody with business before the body is the first red flag — report it, and ask counsel whether you can take part.
itemNotes.d-next-door: Property near a project can gain or lose value from the decision; that is a question for counsel before the item is heard.
itemNotes.d-own-business: Income from a party to the decision is a financial interest, and it is disclosed and counsel consulted before the vote.

options.label: A gift from the applicant whose permit is on the agenda
You and the applicant are registered with the same party
A business you own is the applicant's contractor
Vote now and file the disclosure afterwards
Property you own sits next to the project site

steps.prompt: Select each one that is a financial interest to disclose and ask about — before the item is heard.
steps.title: Practice: mark every interest you raise with counsel before the vote
steps.why: The Political Reform Act and the Form 700 exist so the public can see an official's financial interests before a decision rather than after it. Practising the red flags — a gift from a party, income from a party, property that the decision could change the value of — makes the question to counsel automatic, and the answer, whether to step out, arrives before the vote it would have shaped.

steps.cue: Pick what spending public money in the open requires.

options.label: Put copies on the public table and read the change aloud before testimony continues
Post the revision on the website after the meeting
Carry on — it is only a spreadsheet

steps.prompt: Pick what spending public money in the open requires.
steps.title: Mid-hearing, an aide hands a revised budget sheet to three members. What happens?
steps.why: Documents given to a majority of the body are public at the same time. A revision the public cannot see means residents are testifying against numbers the committee has already replaced — and every vote taken afterwards is in question.

steps.cue: Pick the answer the disclosure rules support.

options.label: Decline, say why, and report any gift you do accept from anyone at its honest value
Accept the applicant's tickets — the permit is weeks away
Accept them and give them to a staff member

steps.prompt: Pick the answer the disclosure rules support.
steps.title: The applicant for next month's permit offers you concert tickets. What do you do?
steps.why: A gift from somebody with business before the body is the plainest conflict there is. Declining it, and valuing and reporting honestly any gift that is accepted from anyone, is what keeps the register meaningful — passing it on to staff only moves the problem.

steps.cue: Select the four parts of owning a hard call in the order they are said.

itemNames.ow-cost: What it costs, and who bears it
itemNames.ow-when: When we will look at it again, in public

options.label: What it costs, and who bears it
What we decided
The staff recommended it, so it is not really on us
When we will look at it again, in public
Why we decided it

steps.outOfOrderNote: What we decided comes first, then why, then the cost, then when we revisit it — a reason given before the decision is named sounds like an excuse.
steps.prompt: Select the four parts of owning a hard call in the order they are said.
steps.title: Practice: build an owned decision statement in order
steps.why: An owned decision is said in a particular order: what we decided, so nobody has to guess; why, so the reasoning can be argued with; what it costs and who bears it, so the people it lands on hear themselves named; and when it will be looked at again in public, so owning it includes a way back. Practising the order is what makes it come out that way at a podium under pressure.

steps.cue: Pick the statement that takes the hard call and owns it.

options.label: "We chose to cut Saturday hours. Here is why, and we revisit it at mid-year, in public."
"The state left us no choice."
Say nothing and let the adopted budget speak for itself

steps.prompt: Pick the statement that takes the hard call and owns it.
steps.title: After a hard budget vote, how does the chair explain the cut?
steps.why: Owning a decision means the first person, the reason and a date to look again. Blaming the state may be partly true and still tells residents the committee will not stand behind its own choice; silence tells them nothing at all.

steps.cue: Pick the answer that helps without taking over.

options.label: Pass her a quiet note with the next step and leave the gavel where it is
Take the gavel back and handle the room yourself
Say nothing and let her work it out alone

steps.prompt: Pick the answer that helps without taking over.
steps.title: Your successor freezes when a resident shouts at her. What does a mentor do?
steps.why: Mentoring the next person means giving her what she needs to act while the authority stays visibly hers. Taking the gavel back teaches the room who is really in charge; leaving her alone teaches her that she was set up to fail.
